title: The Soft Life Trend: How Slowing Down Helped Me Recover From Burnout
summary: The soft life trend taught me more about burnout recovery than any productivity hack ever did. Here’s what slowing down actually looks like in practice.
body_markdown:
## Living a Soft Life in Real Practice


I didn’t overhaul my whole life overnight, that would have been very on-brand for me and very much missing the point. So, I started small. I stopped scheduling things on Sunday mornings. I took my lunch break away from my desk. I started saying “let me check my schedule” instead of automatically saying yes to things. None of them were groundbreaking. But the cumulative effect was.


Over time, I started noticing which parts of my week felt heavy and which felt light. I started asking myself *do I actually want to do this, or do I just feel like I should?* That question alone quietly changed a lot of decisions. I realized, with the help of my therapist, that “shoulding” is a thing I did A LOT, and most of the time, I didn’t even desire the thing I thought I should be doing. I just thought I had to do it because society told me I needed to make more money, work for well-known brands, and burn myself out climbing a ladder that was made up. Learning to push back against those[intrusive thoughts and self-criticism](https://lifestance.com/blog/overcoming-intrusive-negative-thoughts-self-doubt/) was one of the quieter, harder parts of this whole shift.


What I genuinely loved about leaning into a softer approach was how much mental space it freed up. When you’re not constantly in go-mode, you actually get to notice things: what you enjoy, what drains you, and what you’ve been tolerating for way too long.


That said, I’ll be real: there’s a version of the soft life trend that can tip into avoidance, for me. Rest is healthy, but opting out of everything uncomfortable is a different thing. I had to pay attention to whether I was protecting my peace or just hiding from it. For me, the trend worked best as a *corrective* , a way to rebalance after years of over-functioning, rather than a permanent operating mode. I also learned that when my schedule was too open, I got anxious. I worked best with structure, so while that didn’t mean packing my calendar, it meant designating certain times to do certain things. I have a calendar block for play, writing, rest, and meals. And of course, time for work that brings in income. If you tend to spiral when things feel too unstructured, some of these[simple ways to manage anxiety](https://lifestance.com/blog/10-simple-steps-to-manage-anxiety/) are worth bookmarking.
